extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, advertising agencies, marketers, and their legal/compliance counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when advertising and marketing practices run afoul of Section 5 and related rules, with detailed criteria for endorsements, demonstrations, disclosures, promotions, comparative claims, safety claims, country-of-origin claims, and determining ad meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means and Instrumentalities Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies may be liable if they provide others with the means and instrumentalities for engaging in deceptive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies that supply tools, promotional materials, or other instrumentalities used to disseminate deceptive claims can be held accountable (e.g., Castrol, Shell cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of Other Parties (retailers, processors, producers, home shopping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalog marketers, retailers, infomercial producers, home shopping companies, and payment processors may be held liable for their role in making or disseminating deceptive claims or engaging in deceptive trade practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative enforcement actions show payment processors, fulfillment companies, home shopping networks, infomercial producers, retailers, and catalogers have been held liable where they facilitated or disseminated deceptive advertising or assisted fraudulent merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Made through Endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Endorsements and testimonials must not contain representations that would be deceptive or could not be substantiated if made directly by the advertiser; endorsements are not themselves substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because consumers rely on endorsers' opinions, advertisers must possess competent and reliable evidence to support the underlying efficacy representations conveyed by endorsements. Any material connection between endorser and advertiser that might affect credibility must be disclosed (Guides Concerning Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising, 16 C.F.R. § 255).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Endorsers
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals or institutions represented to be experts must have qualifications sufficient to give the represented expertise and must support an expert endorsement with testing or examination at least as extensive as experts in the field would agree is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: 'an individual, group, or institution possessing ... knowledge of a particular subject, which knowledge is superior to that generally acquired by ordinary individuals' (16 C.F.R. § 255.0(d)). Both advertiser and expert endorser can be held liable for deceptive representations. Examples include physician or other professional endorsements challenged when unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Endorsers / Testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer testimonials are generally interpreted to convey that the endorser’s experience is representative of what consumers will typically achieve; if not, advertisers must clearly disclose the limited applicability or the generally expected performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A blanket disclaimer like 'Not all consumers will get this result' is insufficient to cure a misleading testimonial. Anecdotal evidence is generally inadequate to substantiate efficacy claims (see examples such as weight-loss ear clip case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity Endorsers
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity endorsements must reflect the honest opinions, findings, beliefs, or experience of the celebrity; advertisers must substantiate claims made by celebrities and ensure a celebrity represented to use the product is a bona fide user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers may use an endorsement only as long as they have good reason to believe the endorser continues to subscribe to the views presented. Courts have held celebrity endorsers to the requisite level of substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Made Through Demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Product demonstrations must accurately depict how the product will perform under normal consumer use; demonstrations altered to misrepresent a material attribute are deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ad is deceptive if demonstration techniques (off-camera tricks, doctored props, artificial conditions) falsely depict typical performance. Representative cases show before-and-after photos and staged demos can violate Section 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Truthful references to competitors or competing products are encouraged, but comparative ads require clarity and, if necessary, appropriate disclosures to avoid deception (Statement of Policy Regarding Comparative Advertising, 16 C.F.R. § 14.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative claims that imply superiority must be accurate and not misleading about relative performance, nutrition, strength, etc.; the Commission enforces against deceptive comparative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and Risk-Reduction Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers must have reliable substantiation to support safety-related or risk reduction claims and must carefully qualify claims to indicate the level of safety or significant risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about preventing disease, detecting pathogens, blocking radiation, or materially reducing risk require competent and reliable scientific evidence; enforcement examples include cell phone shields, do-it-yourself test kits, and health remedies. When material health risks exist from misuse, warnings and labeling may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Made in U.S.A. Claims Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission retains the 'all or virtually all' standard for merchandise advertised or labeled as 'Made in U.S.A.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Businesses making country-of-origin claims should follow the FTC's published guide 'Complying with the Made in USA Standard.' Representative cases show enforcement for false 'Made in USA' labeling and significant penalties or consent orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotions (Coupons, Rebates, Gift Cards, 'Free' Offers, Continuity Plans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations about promotions are subject to the same standards of truthfulness and accuracy as other product claims and may also implicate the Mail or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule, Telemarketing Sales Rule, Negative Option Rule, and the Unordered Merchandise Statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must clearly disclose material terms (e.g., dormancy fees, expiration policies, costs hidden behind 'free' offers). Failure to deliver rebates or unambiguous terms has led to enforcement actions and consumer redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebates — Timeliness and Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebate programs must deliver on promised timing and disclose any delays or conditions; misrepresenting rebate timeframes or failing to honor rebates is deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases challenge delayed rebate issuance, failure to disclose long waits to submit rebate requests, and unilateral modifications to rebate programs after advertising has begun. The FTC has sponsored workshops on complying with applicable laws when advertising rebates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Forms of Promotion — Negative Option and 'Free' Sample Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering 'free' samples or trials that enroll consumers in ongoing paid programs, debiting accounts without authorization, or burying costs in licensing agreements can be deceptive and violate negative option and electronic funds rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must make clear and conspicuous disclosures of any material terms that convert a 'free' trial into a paid membership and must obtain express informed consent before charging consumers. Representative enforcement includes cases bringing civil penalties and redress for undisclosed billing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising Directed at Spanish-Speaking Consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing targeted to Spanish-speaking/Hispanic consumers must comply with the same truthfulness standards and requires outreach and appropriately tailored compliance efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC has conducted workshops and enforcement initiatives focused on protecting Hispanic consumers and has pursued actions against deceptive Spanish-language telemarketing and advertising. Examples include deceptive representations on national Spanish-language television and telemarketing prizing schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Ad Meaning — Express Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Express claims unequivocally state the representation and the representation itself establishes the meaning of the claim; no further proof about the meaning is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When language or depictions expressly state a claim, the Commission treats that stated claim as the ad's meaning (Deception Policy Statement; Thompson Medical Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Ad Meaning — Implied Claims Continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied claims are those not expressly stated and range from language virtually synonymous with an express claim to subtle suggestions that few consumers would interpret as making the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission recognizes a continuum for implied claims and will consider the ad's overall context in deciding whether an implied claim is conveyed (Kraft, Thompson Medical Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Implied Claims — Net Impression / Whole-Ad Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether reasonable consumers are likely to take an implied claim, the Commission looks at the net impression created by the ad as a whole — 'the entire mosaic, rather than each tile separately.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider visuals, text, audio, sequencing, and any juxtaposed elements to discern the ad's net impression (Deception Policy Statement; Stouffer Foods Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic Evidence for Implied Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When an implied claim is not clear enough from the ad alone, extrinsic evidence (e.g., copy tests, marketing expert testimony, evidence of intent) may be required to establish that the ad conveys the implied claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extrinsic evidence is available, the Commission will consider its relative quality and reliability. The Commission has applied this approach in cases where ad content alone was ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy Tests — Reliability Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy tests (consumer research eliciting the claims consumers took from an ad) may be used as extrinsic evidence but must be methodologically sound to be reliable and probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appropriate standard is not perfection but whether the evidence is reliable and probative; methodological flaws can reduce weight but do not automatically exclude copy tests if they provide probative evidence (Kraft; Thompson Medical; Stouffer Foods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Forms of Extrinsic Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Other extrinsic evidence can include testimony by marketing experts on how consumers respond to particular ad presentations and evidence of the advertiser's intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission will weigh such evidence by its quality and reliability when determining whether an implied claim is conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures in Ads — Cannot Cure Contradictory Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers cannot use fine print to contradict other statements in an ad or to cure misimpressions created by more prominent ad elements; accurate fine print may not remedy a false headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures must be clear and conspicuous; courts have required simultaneous audio/visual disclosures in some contexts. The Commission has convened workshops and issued policy statements reiterating the 'clear and conspicuous' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures Effectiveness Factors (Prominence, Presentation, Placement, Proximity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating the effectiveness of disclosures, the Commission considers prominence, presentation (easy-to-understand language and timing), placement (format/location consumers will read or hear), and proximity to the claim being qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures that are inconspicuous, confusing, placed far from the claim, or presented at times when consumers' attention is distracted will likely be ineffective. The FTC has guidance and workshop findings on effective disclosures (e.g., Disclosure Exposure; Dot Com Disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Print Disclosures — Fine Print Often Inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-print footnotes or blocks of text in print ads and point-of-sale materials frequently fail to adequately disclaim or modify claims made elsewhere in the promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative cases show fine-print notes placed down the side of ads or in inconspicuous locations have been found inadequate to disclose material limitations or costs (e.g., online service add-ons, 'free' internet offers, sodium content or '98% fat free' claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Television Disclosures — Superscripts and Readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Video superscripts that are difficult to understand, superimposed over distracting backgrounds, compete with audio elements, or are placed in parts of the ad less likely to be remembered are ineffective to modify claims in the body of the ad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For important qualifying information in TV ads, simultaneous audio and visual disclosure or other prominent techniques may be required; mere small or fast superscripts often will not suffice (Thompson Medical Co.).
